newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cert coffee stocks fall to new all-time low.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cert coffee stocks fall to new all-time low.

text.p: U.S. certified coffee stocks fell by 4,036 60-kg bags in the week ended October 25, to 1,547 bags, the lowest level since the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange began tracking inventories in 1980.
No coffee was reported pending grading or recertification, the CSCE said Monday.

The steep drawdown included the reinstatement of 150 bags of Salvadorean certified coffee to the exchange's New Orleans warehouses following a reporting error on part of one warehouse that was revealed last week, the CSCE said.

Last week, CSCE said the certified stock total of 5,583 bags reported as of October 18 was correct, but that the sharp 24,391-bag drawdown in warehouse certified coffee stocks initially reported was attributable to "past errors in reporting".
While many operators said they had anticipated a small decline this week, they had not expected a drop equivalent to about 70 percent of total stocks.
"It is a very, very low level of stocks," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast. "There will probably be panic buying tomorrow. It is really going to worry the specs."

Prendergast said the market's furor could increase with only about three weeks to go until the spot December contract goes into its month-long notice period. December coffee, which goes off the board December 18, had 12,524 lots open interest as of Friday's close, equivalent to more than three million bags of coffee.
Most traders agree the nearby switch, which ballooned to 13.25 cents Monday, would benefit most by the low stock level.
"I am a bit surprised," one trader said. "It is positive news and should bring us up to the highs of last week. But I think the switch will react the most.
But other traders said that while the draw underscored the tight near-term supply situation, it should have come as no surprise.
"It was all sold beforehand," one trader said. "It really should not matter."

They noted that more Colombian coffee should start to flow slowly into the market following the end of a truckers' strike Thursday. And many Central American countries, which have had difficulty getting their beans to port due to flooding from recent heavy rainfall, should begin exporting coffee in the coming weeks.
-- Patricia Avidan, New York Commodities Desk, +1 212 859 1640
